The Scottish Borders: Riding Scotland Without the Crowds

The Scottish Borders is the forgotten region between Edinburgh and the English border. While tourists flock to the Highlands, the Borders offers quiet roads, rolling hills, historic abbey towns, and some of the finest riding in Scotland — all without the tourist traffic. It's a region that rewards repeat visits and reveals its character slowly.

The Abbey Towns

Four magnificent medieval abbeys form the heart of the Borders: Jedburgh, Melrose, Dryburgh, and Kelso. Each is dramatically ruined and atmospheric, and the towns around them have excellent facilities for touring riders. Melrose is the most charming, with boutique shops, good restaurants, and the atmospheric Melrose Abbey where Robert the Bruce's heart is buried.

The Great Outdoors

The Borders landscape is rolling hills and river valleys. The Tweed, Teviot, Yarrow, and Ettrick rivers create a network of green valleys connected by flowing roads. The Southern Uplands rise to modest heights but create a landscape of sweeping moorland and empty ridges. Mountain biking trails in the Tweed Valley (Glentress, Innerleithen) have transformed the region's outdoor reputation.

Best Borders Bases

  • Melrose — Charming abbey town, excellent restaurants, central location. The Townhouse Hotel is recommended
  • Peebles — Elegant town on the Tweed, good shops and pubs. Gateway to the Tweed Valley trails
  • Hawick — Industrial heritage town with genuine character. Home to textile mills and rugby
  • Moffat — Gateway to the Grey Mare's Tail and the Devil's Beeftub. The Moffat Toffee Shop is an institution

What to See and Do

Abbotsford House — Sir Walter Scott's baronial fantasy home on the Tweed, beautifully restored and open to visitors. Traquair House — Scotland's oldest inhabited house, with its own brewery producing excellent ales. Grey Mare's Tail — 60-metre waterfall visible from the A708, one of Scotland's tallest.

The Borders is Scotland's best-value motorcycle destination. Accommodation is cheaper than the Highlands, the roads are emptier, and the scenery — while less dramatic — is beautiful in a gentler, more human way.

Events

The Borders towns hold Common Riding festivals throughout summer — horse-riding events that celebrate ancient boundaries. These lively festivals combine pageantry, community spirit, and serious celebration. Hawick's Common Riding in June is the most famous. The Borders Book Festival in Melrose (June) is one of Scotland's best literary events.

Practical Information

The Borders is well-connected by road — the A7 from Edinburgh to Carlisle and the A68 from Edinburgh to Darlington provide fast north-south links. Fuel is available in all towns. Accommodation is plentiful and reasonably priced. The region is accessible from Edinburgh (1 hour), Newcastle (90 minutes), and Glasgow (90 minutes). Best months: April-October.

faq.q: Why choose the Scottish Borders over the Highlands?
faq.a: The Borders is Scotland's best-value motorcycle destination. Accommodation is cheaper than the Highlands, the roads are emptier, and while the scenery is less dramatic it is beautiful in a gentler, more human way. Tourists flock north, leaving the Borders quiet and rewarding for riders who prefer flowing roads without heavy traffic.

faq.q: What are the abbey towns worth visiting?
faq.a: Four magnificent medieval abbeys form the heart of the Borders: Jedburgh, Melrose, Dryburgh and Kelso. Each is dramatically ruined and atmospheric, and the towns around them have excellent facilities for touring riders. Melrose is the most charming, with the abbey where Robert the Bruce's heart is buried.

faq.q: Where is the best base for exploring the Borders?
faq.a: Melrose is a charming abbey town with excellent restaurants and a central location, and the Townhouse Hotel is recommended. Peebles is an elegant town on the Tweed with good shops and pubs, while Moffat is the gateway to the Grey Mare's Tail waterfall and the Devil's Beeftub.

faq.q: How do I get to the Scottish Borders?
faq.a: The Borders is well-connected by road, with the A7 from Edinburgh to Carlisle and the A68 from Edinburgh to Darlington providing fast north-south links. The region is accessible from Edinburgh in about an hour, Newcastle in 90 minutes and Glasgow in 90 minutes. Fuel is available in all the main towns.

faq.q: What are the Common Riding festivals?
faq.a: The Borders towns hold Common Riding festivals throughout summer, horse-riding events that celebrate ancient boundaries with pageantry, community spirit and serious celebration. Hawick's Common Riding in June is the most famous. If you visit during one, expect busy towns and a lively atmosphere, so book accommodation ahead.
